title: ASML posts record Q3 2026 and raises full-year outlook as AI capex pulls through
subtitle: The Dutch lithography monopoly reported €11.7 billion in Q3 net sales and guided Q4 to €14.2–15.2 billion, with full-year 2026 revenue now expected to land between €44 and €45 billion.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: ASML reported third-quarter 2026 results on October 14 that beat its own guidance across the board. Total net sales came in at €11.7 billion against a guided range of €11.0–12.0 billion, with €8.4 billion in new systems and €3.3 billion in Installed Base Management. Net income was €5.0 billion, gross margin was 57.5 percent, and basic earnings per share were €12.95. The company guided Q4 net sales to €14.2–15.2 billion and raised its full-year 2026 outlook to €44–45 billion, up from the €43–45 billion range it gave in July.

The read-through to AI matters because ASML sells the only extreme-ultraviolet lithography systems in the world, which means every leading-edge AI accelerator — Nvidia's Rubin GPUs, Google's TPU v8i, Meta's Iris, AMD's MI450 — passes through its tools. The Q3 bookings print and the raised full-year guide are therefore the cleanest proxy available for whether the hyperscalers' announced $700-billion-plus 2026 capex plans are translating into real orders at the foundry level, not just slide-deck commitments.

The context is a quarter in which TSMC's September revenue rose 54.6 percent year-over-year and its Q3 revenue hit a record NT$1.49 trillion — numbers Reuters attributed directly to AI demand. Those two companies sit on opposite ends of the same supply chain: ASML sells the machines, TSMC runs them, Nvidia and others buy the wafers. When both post record quarters in the same week, it tells investors that AI spending is still pulling hardware through the pipeline rather than piling up as unused capacity.

A takeaway for learners: the earliest and most honest indicator of whether AI spending is real is not model benchmarks or chatbot usage charts — it is upstream capital-equipment orders. By the time money gets to ASML and TSMC, intent has turned into dollars, and the lag between order and revenue is long enough that these prints reflect decisions made months ago. Watch bookings and backlog, not revenue, for the next turn in the cycle.
